newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Jiang vows to purse Deng Xiaoping reforms.
newsitem.headline: China's Jiang vows to purse Deng Xiaoping reforms.

text.p: President Jiang Zemin offered unstinted praise for Deng Xiaoping in a funeral oration on Tuesday, telling 10,000 of China's elite the future lay with the profound economic reforms pioneered by the deceased strongman.

As final rites began for Deng, who died last Wednesday aged 92, sirens and whistles wailed nationwide for three minutes in deference to the man who delivered unprecedented prosperity to the world's most populous nation while keeping communists in charge.

In Beijing's cavernous Great Hall of the People, Mao-suited revolutionaries mingled with Western-suited technocrats to hear Jiang, Deng's protege and now China's most powerful man, sob theatrically at the start of an hour-long eulogy.
"The people of China love Comrade Deng Xiaoping...we cherish the memory of Comrade Deng Xiaoping," Jiang said.
"Reform is the inevitable road through which China will be able to achieve socialist modernisation," Jiang said, reaffirming the distinctive Deng formula of economic reform mixed with socialism.

On the stage beneath a black-framed portrait of a smiling, avuncular Deng lay a casket containing his ashes, draped with a red hammer-and-sickle communist flag and surrounded by flowers and a wreath from his grief-stricken family.

But in hosannas to the lifelong communist who forged a fledgling economic superpower out of a Stalinist backwater, Jiang glossed over what many see as Deng's darkest hour -- his 1989 use of the army to crush pro-democracy protests centred on Tiananmen Square. "We withstood the severe test," he said.
On Tuesday, in the vast square adjoining the Great Hall, Beijing's authoritarian hand was in evidence.
Police cleared the square soon after dawn, throwing a security net over an arena that is a potent symbol of China and a focus for expressions of grief as well as demonstrations of anger.
One small group of people who unfurled a banner of mourning were quickly asked to leave and police ushered away a weeping elderly couple who tried to lay a wreath.

On the Beijing Commodity Exchange, traders shut down their computer terminals and stood with heads bowed out of respect to Deng, who introduced all manner of capitalist-style innovations, from stocks and bonds to pawn shops and night clubs.
Jiang seized upon the eulogy and emotional displays for the deceased patriarch to remind his opponents, and the 1.2 billion people over whom he now holds sway, that he is in charge, diplomats said.
"Under the party's leadership with Jiang Zemin as its core, carry out the unfulfilled wishes of Deng Xiaoping," read a banner hanging from a balcony in the Great Hall.
Jiang issued his strongest pledge yet to recover the island of Taiwan, an achievement that had eluded Deng and Mao.
"The Taiwan question will be settled eventually and the complete reunification of the motherland will certainly be achieved," Jiang promised.

The man who holds China's top three jobs -- party chief, state president and commander-in-chief of the armed forces -- assured the three-million-strong People's Liberation Army that they would not be forgotten as China races to modernise.
Analysts say the support of the military is essential for Jiang's survival as he emerges from seven years under the wing of his powerful patron.
On Monday, television showed China's millions indelible images of their dead leader lying in state, his face pale and puffy. It was the first glimpse of their ruler in three years.
It was the sort of lingering display of his remains that Deng -- contemptuous of the personality cult around his predecessor Mao Zedong -- had forbidden.
"Deng looked at peace," the Xinhua news agency said.
Political analysts questioned, however, whether the patriarch would have been at ease with the way his successors have handled the delicate transition period.
